turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the eleventh of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Today: one official in Washington switched the dollar off for an international court, and on for Russian diesel. Same afternoon. Same signature.
[curious] A tax table in Tokyo that spent thirty-two years writing the nation's beer recipes — and then deleted its own invention.
And a sock. Specifically, the one-dollar difference between a good sock and an expensive one.
[amused] You say that like it's a let-down. It is genuinely the best thing in the book.
It's the spine of the whole issue, actually. We called it the toll.
What gets charged for permission.
And how seldom the charge matches the thing. Start with the biggest one.
Friday afternoon, Washington. Walk me through it.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control publishes a document two paragraphs long. It's called General Licence number one hundred and thirty-five. It authorises the sale, delivery, offloading and importation — including importation into the United States — of diesel fuel of Russian Federation origin.
And the timestamp is the part you keep circling.
[deadpan] Two forty-three in the afternoon and fifty-nine seconds. Signed by the director of that office.
Why does the second hand matter?
Because the same office, under the same action date, had just put the International Criminal Court on the sanctions list. Not a judge. The institution, at its address.
So the dollar's plumbing gets switched off for a court and on for a sanctioned exporter, in one afternoon, by one person.
That's the sentence.
Okay — and the diesel itself? How much are we talking?

Announced by post. Over three hundred thousand tonnes immediately, five hundred thousand in November, a million after that, and up to three million if refineries allow. Moscow moved on Saturday — the cabinet partially lifted its own export ban on the identical ladder.
[thoughtful] That sounds enormous.
It is not enormous. Take October and November together — eight hundred thousand tonnes. Roughly six million barrels.
And America burns?
About three point seven million barrels of diesel a day.
[pause] So the entire announcement is... a day and a half.
Thirty-six hours of American consumption.
Why do it, then?
Because the pump is the politics. American retail diesel is six dollars and twenty-eight cents a gallon. A year ago it was three dollars sixty-seven.
[exhales] Up seventy-one per cent.
In a year. And that's the thing to understand about this whole week — crude was quiet. Brent sat near a hundred and four. It's the refined product that broke.
So the sceptic's case is: trivially small, and it may not even arrive.

Worse than that. Russian diesel exports fell from eight hundred and fifty thousand barrels a day in the first quarter to one hundred and ninety thousand in the third. Russia imported diesel this quarter.
And politically it detonated.
On Saturday the President told Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries. Quote: so he better damn well stop. And then: I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president.
[skeptical] And Kyiv?

Zelensky had already called the licence a weak decision by our strong partners. After a daytime missile attack he wrote that the consequences of allowing Russia to sell oil products were most clearly felt in Kyiv that day.
[sighs] Right.
One more from the World desk, because it's the opposite kind of story. Panama.
And the actual count?
By Saturday night: twenty-seven injured. Nobody killed.
Okay. The money block. And I want to start with the weirdest chart of the week.
Gold rose with the dollar. Bitcoin did not.
Say more.

Gold was up one point three per cent on the week, to four thousand two hundred and sixteen dollars on the exchange. And it rose while the dollar index was up, and while the ten-year sat at five point two four per cent.
[thoughtful] Two things sold as the same hedge, going opposite ways in the same five sessions.
That's the week's most informative signal.
What's driving all of it?

One force, and it's diesel, not oil in the abstract. And a central bank cannot ease against a supply shock. The Federal Reserve's September minutes name the mechanism in their own words — geopolitics pushed up prices for crude oil and refined fuel products — and most participants assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate by year end.
[scoffs] That's nothing. And they still want to hike.
Because the shock is on the supply side. Staff don't see two per cent inflation until twenty twenty-nine.
What does that do to a plain global portfolio?

The bond leg is the problem. A global aggregate bond fund made one tenth of one per cent on the week while ten-year yields actually fell. A bond that can't make money on a rate rally has no convexity left to give.
Ah — so that's the Singapore read.
Nearly seven per cent below its September record. Thursday alone took a hundred and ninety-five points.
And Wednesday is the date to mark.

Wednesday. The Monetary Authority of Singapore publishes its Monetary Policy Statement on the fourteenth, confirmed on its own calendar, with the Macroeconomic Review the same day. A third tightening of the year is widely expected.
[curious] And yet?

And yet the Singapore dollar sits a touch weaker on the month. Tightening the band against a global dollar bid is tightening uphill. That's the question to put on Wednesday. None of this is advice, and a forecast is a forecast.
Staying in Singapore — Parliament did something genuinely novel this week.
It went after the advertisement rather than the vehicle.
[amused] So listing it is now as serious as smuggling it.
And the reason is a number: forty-nine active-mobility device fires last year.
What about the haze? It's still here, I can see it from my window.
Not cleared. At five this morning the twenty-four hour index read a hundred and fifty-five in the Central region. Unhealthy everywhere, but below Friday's peak of a hundred and ninety-two.
[skeptical] Is three hundred even reachable?
That is exactly what a HardwareZone forum thread spent Saturday evening saying. One poster: don't think the official reading would reach this figure. Another joked it will stay at two ninety-nine.
So you can be told to avoid all outdoor activity on one dial while the other dial is nowhere near the closure line.
That's the sceptic's case, and it's sound.
Technology. There's a jury out right now.
In Delaware. Qualcomm against Arm, five days of trial, and on Friday the jury deliberated about four hours and went home. They come back Tuesday — two days after this issue printed.
What are they actually deciding?
What a company may charge for permission to design a chip. An architecture licence is the closest thing this industry has to a border.
[curious] And the money?

There's a clause nobody has ruled on under which Qualcomm could stop paying royalties for five years if Arm breached. And Qualcomm's chief executive testified that the increase Arm wants for the next instruction set is eighteen hundred per cent.
[gasps] Eighteen hundred?
One outlet carries that figure and the newswire carries no damages number at all. So take the scale, not the decimal.
[excited] That's more than double.
And then somebody with two older cards measured it. Single card: a gain of one to five per cent. Two cards: twenty-five to thirty-four per cent slower.
[deadpan] Slower.
A flat regression. And the same pattern repeated on a second merge three days later — the person who reproduced it found a smaller number than the person who wrote it. Both times.
The Kit. You've got a watch I think you want to warn me off.
[wry] Garmin's Enduro four. Nine hundred dollars, announced on the sixth. And the most useful fact about it is that Garmin appears not to have sent out review units.
[laughs] That is the review.

The owners' forum got there first. One: the band is legit the only thing that's clearly different when you hold them side by side. Another, just: I can see a pretty big difference — a hundred dollars.
What does the hundred buy?
Thirty-two more gigabytes, a map view, a better strap, and thirty seconds off calculating a route on the wrist. Almost everything else arrives on the old watch by software update.
[chuckles] On the same page.
On the same page.
Right — the Atelier. Socks. Convince me.
Gauge is the number of latch needles standing around the cylinder of a knitting machine. Needles on a drum, not stitches per inch of cloth.
So what do I actually look for?
The toe. It's either cut and sewn, which leaves a ridge you can feel, or it's linked — re-knitted loop by loop for a flat join.
And the price difference between those two?
In one maker's own range, about a dollar.
And there's a trap in the vocabulary.

A real one. This desk set out to explain that a Rosso toe is the premium hand-linked finish. The one trade source we could read says the reverse — that rosso is the overlocked ridge, cheapest and fastest, the default for most commercial production.
[skeptical] So if I walk into a shop and ask for a Rosso toe —
You may be asking for the cheap one. Ask whether the toe is linked. Run a thumb across it.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every week with this one.
Who does this?

Here's the post that opens the desk, from the thirtieth of September. Quote: I am forty-four, and after a long pause in skateboarding I started longboarding mostly because I just want to cruise and not break my bones in the process.
[warmly] That's lovely.
He posted five more times in nine days. Stability, then wheels, then exercises for the soles of his feet, then which of two boards to buy.
[laughs] The whole arc of falling in, in public.
And the demographic isn't in dispute. The flagship long-distance wheel is called the Dad Bod.
Okay, I'm in. How big is this world?
Smaller than anyone admits. One research firm puts the global skateboard market at three point seven billion dollars. Another puts the same market at one point five six billion.
[scoffs] Those aren't close.

Neither publishes a longboard figure at all. The honest answer is nobody credibly measures this. The real evidence is sadder — a Bristol shop reported in September that one wheel was out of stock across the whole of Europe.
What does the gear cost?
This is where it inverts everything cycling taught you. The deck is the cheap part. There's no frame, and the trucks cost more.
Give me a number.
A properly specified complete board: three hundred and forty to three hundred and ninety US dollars. And the meaningful upgrades after that are bushings and bearings, which run in tens of dollars.
[amused] And he publishes his sponsors.
He does, to his credit. And on one newer truck brand he writes that he cannot tell whether the maker is authentic or a copycat — the waters feels very mudded.
So the money pit isn't the board.
It's a treadmill of ten-dollar decisions that feels like engineering.
Now — the Singapore bit. Can you actually do this here?

[excited] This is the finding, and it's the opposite of everywhere else. Under the transport authority's own device matrix, a non-motorised device — explicitly skateboards and kick-scooters — may be ridden on cycling paths and footpaths. No registration, no theory test, no minimum age.
[gasps] So the pushed board has more legal access than the electric one.

Everywhere else, e-boards ate the commute. Here the law fenced them. And if you've got a twelve-year-old, you can legally ride the same footpaths together on pushed boards. You could not do that on e-scooters.
That's genuinely useful. What's the catch?
Heat, and fragility. The sport's great forum returns a server error. One famous brand's domain doesn't resolve at all. The governing body's news stopped in January last year.
[thoughtful] So it's not that it got expensive.

Where gravel cyclists complain their sport got rich, longboarders complain theirs got thin. And the threads have already solved the heat — their post titles this fortnight are Out before the sunrise, Flashlights on Friday, and Midnight Marathon.
Culture and the body. Quickly.
A horror film called Other Mommy took twelve point six million dollars on Friday alone — and sits at eighteen per cent with critics.
[wry] They all arrived at once, after the money.

And my favourite thing is that the critics and the audience wrote the same review. A professional complained it had filched so many of its good ideas from elsewhere. A user on Letterboxd, one star, put it in seven words: I ordered Coraline on Temu and this is what I got.
[laughs] Perfect.
The Good Life: Bremont's new ceramic diver. Its product page says the edition is limited to two hundred and fifty pieces.
[deadpan] So the scarcity is free.
Scarcity that commands no premium is a production run with a number attached.
And at twelve to thirteen?
More externalising behaviour, and more odd perceptual experiences. And no effect on internalising. Not anxiety, not low mood — the one thing parents actually fear is the thing it did not find.
[curious] How big are these effects?

Tiny. And so was the screen-time effect we printed a fortnight ago — four hundredths of a standard deviation. Professor Candice Odgers has the line: the field's efforts have produced a mix of no, small and mixed associations.
And the long read. This one I loved.
[thoughtful] Japan. On the first of October, the Japanese state stopped writing beer recipes.
So brewers engineered to the tax line.
They engineered to the notch. The industry called the result new genre. Shoppers called it third beer. It wasn't a recipe anyone wanted — it was the shape of a tax notch, filled in.
[curious] And the ministry said why?
In its own chart. It wrote that the rate gaps between similar liquors were affecting product development and sales volumes.
[pause] A finance ministry writing down that its tax had been designing the nation's drinks.

Almost nobody outside Japan has noticed that one did. And the tax agency's own volume tables show what it cost. Beer ran seven point four million kilolitres in the nineteen ninety-four fiscal year. By twenty twenty-four it was two point five.
And the first days after the switch?
Beer units up nineteen and a half per cent. Happoshu down more than a quarter. New genre down thirty-five per cent.
[laughs] They were just waiting for Thursday.

And here's the second act nobody has joined to the first. Six days after every brewer in Japan repriced its entire range on the same morning, the competition regulator opened a criminal cartel investigation into all four of them. And raided the brewers' trade association itself.
[gasps] Not just the companies. The room where they meet.
For thirty-two years they didn't need to collude on product design, because the tax table did it for them. Four companies reading the same notch arrive at the same recipe without a conversation.
[thoughtful] And the moment you remove the table —
Is the first moment a regulator can tell the difference between a cartel and a tax.
So what does it mean? Give me the argument.
Ask the drinkers. The brewers' own survey asked what people would drink instead of new genre once it got dearer. Fifty-six per cent said they would not increase any other alcohol at all.
[pause] More than half just leave.

People drink beer because it tastes good — about three quarters say so. They drank the cheap tier because the price was reasonable. Those aren't two preferences about flavour. That's a preference and a constraint.
Remove the constraint's relief —
And you don't create a beer drinker. You create an ex-drinker.
[drawn out] Hm.

And the honest counter is that beer was falling anyway — down three per cent in the first half of this year, down seven per cent in July alone. So the test is clean and it comes soon. If the November and December supermarket numbers hold beer above last year once the stockpiles are drunk, the reform moved people.
[thoughtful] That's the toll again, isn't it. Charged for permission to drink the cheap thing.
Every finance ministry contemplating simplification should read this one.
That's a hell of a closer.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
